suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
conditional rather than per-project edits.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
  artifact derives from it.
- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.

## A stamp, not a name

The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.

## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides

Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**

- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
  presentation, docs, notes.
- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).

**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.

## Grammar and storage

One spelling everywhere the version is written:

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
  version storable in every medium below.
- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability, while manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a
  leading `v`. Cargo rejects one.)

Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:

- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
  valid at any dot depth.
- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
  adds its case to
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).

Two reservations keep the remap sound:

- **The stored version identifies but does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out), while PEP 440 sorts the
  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.

**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
`+` are all invalid. `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth. `1.2.3-1` parses but
silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
every medium accepts.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
the case that fits your medium:

- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
    ...). Add the case as needed
- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
  per-commit preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
  flow's install.

Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
its `custom.md` layer.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
neither a number nor a version (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
above, every commit carries a distinct version.

1	# Cycle protocol
2	
3	This protocol uses [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form). It
4	contains instructions on how a commit cycle is accomplished.
5	
6	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed
7	change is edited here and converges at the template
8	([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
9	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
10	
11	The artifact a cycle produces is whatever the bot generates from
12	the conversation: code, prose, an image, a song, a screenplay.
13	The steps below use a Rust crate as the running example (the
14	cargo cycle, `Cargo.toml` versioning). Substitute your medium's
15	equivalents. This project's manifest is recorded in
16	[versioning.md](versioning.md).
17	
18	## Cycles
19	
20	A cycle has three phases:
21	
22	- **[Preparation](#preparation)**: the cycle's first commit,
23	  when it needs setup (a lightweight cycle omits it and
24	  starts at its first Work step). Sets up the cycle:
25	  - Bump the version-of-record (where it lives and the
26	    suffix scheme are project-specific, per
27	    [versioning.md](versioning.md)).
28	  - Pick up a `## Todo` item (typically the top-ranked, #1)
29	    into `## In Progress` as the cycle's
30	    [six provisional items](#preparation): title, problem
31	    statement, solution statement, acceptance check, ladder,
32	    deliberation.
33	  - Create the cycle's topic bookmark.
34	  - Nothing is opened in the chores file. The block is the
35	    cycle's only home until close-out moves it.
36	- **[Work-N](#work-n)**: the commits that implement the
37	  change. As many as the change needs. Each runs through the
38	  [per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow).
39	- **[Close-out](#close-out)**: the cycle's last commit.
40	  Bookkeeping only:
41	  - Run the acceptance check and record what it showed.
42	  - Finalize the six items, then move the block into
43	    `notes/chores/`, which creates the
44	    [chores section](#chores-sections).
45	  - Write the `## Done` entry and clear `## In Progress`.
46	  - Land the cycle's bookmark.
47	  - Optionally update `notes/README.md` if functionality
48	    changed.
49	
50	A cycle's commits are published to the project remote
51	either incrementally or as one batch at close-out. The
52	result must always be published at close-out. See
53	[Pushing](#pushing).
54	
55	**Sub-cycles.** When a Work commit's scope grows enough to
56	warrant its own ladder, it subdivides into its own
57	Preparation / Work / Close-out. The same three-phase shape
58	applies recursively at every depth, and a sub-ladder's rungs
59	are titles like any other. See
60	[Step naming](#step-naming) for how a step is identified and
61	[Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the local-ladder
62	mechanics.
63	
64	## Chores sections
65	
66	A **chores section** is a `##` section in `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` recording landed work.
67	In general, every commit that lands on the permanent branch should have a rung in some
68	section's as-built ladder in a chores file.
69	
70	**A cycle's record has one home at a time.** While the cycle runs it lives entirely in
71	`TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the [six provisional items](#preparation) written at Preparation
72	and revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block **moves** into the chores file, becoming
73	that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in two places, so there is nothing to keep in
74	sync and nothing to write twice.
75	
76	The move is mechanical, four transforms and no rewriting:
77	
78	- **Heading levels shift so the title becomes the section's `##`** and the items shift with it,
79	  staying one level under the title. Anchors survive untouched, because GitHub slugs derive from
80	  the heading's *text*, not its level. The depth shift is one level for a plain cycle, and
81	  whatever the title's depth demands under a program heading.
82	- **Rung refs renumber** into the destination file's `[N]` namespace (see
83	  [Reference numbering](notes.md#reference-numbering)).
84	- **Repo-root-relative links gain `../`**, since the block moves from the root into
85	  `notes/chores/`.
86	- **The block's own forward-looking notes are rewritten**, since they described a future that
87	  has now happened.
88	
89	Two of those fail *silently*: a mis-renumbered ref and an un-rebased link render as plain text
90	or a 404 rather than erroring. Check both by hand until a `validate-repo` exists.
91	
92	A single-commit cycle's ladder is one rung, its close-out. Rung placeholders are backfilled once
93	the commit is permanent (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) below).
94	
95	The move also appends the section's title-only `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry to the file's
96	`## Table of Contents`.
97	
98	Adopted after a full-cycle trial: the dual maintenance disappeared, and the narrative did not
99	thin out from being written in `TODO.md`, which was the watched-for risk.
100	
101	Fuller chores conventions (content rules, header sync, design subsection pattern, ladder and
102	reference formatting, the Table of Contents) live in
103	[Chores conventions](notes.md#chores-conventions).
104	
105	### Commits backfill
106	
107	An as-built ladder rung cites its commit by SHA and records the version that commit carried,
108	and neither is stable until the commit lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a long-lived
109	release/patch branch that won't be rewritten). A rebase or squash rewrites the SHA and may
110	renumber the version on the way. So:
111	
112	- A rung is **written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version**.
113	- **Backfill once the commit is on a permanent branch**, where both are final. A commit
114	  can't record its own SHA (that would change the hash), so the fill always lands one push
115	  later: **each push backfills the rungs of the commits the previous push made permanent.** On
116	  a topic branch the sections instead wait until the branch lands, so nothing is ever written
117	  that a later rebase could invalidate.
118	- A deliberate rewrite of already-recorded commits (a coordinated re-describe, a retroactive
119	  reshape) invalidates their recorded SHAs. Re-record them once the rewrite is published, on
120	  the same one-push-later timing.
121	
122	Backfill replaces the placeholder with a real file-local `[N]` slot, defined as the commit URL +
123	40-hex SHA in the file's `# References` (format in
124	[Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)), and writes the version ahead of
125	the title. A section's `##` title matches its close-out commit title, and each rung's text its
126	own commit title, so a rare deliberate rewrite of a permanent-branch commit re-syncs via
127	`git log --grep "<title>"`. Sections that predate the ladder form keep their grandfathered
128	`Commits:` lines. Backfill those where they exist.
129	
130	The per-push cadence is a project choice, not dogma. A **per-close-out** model (recording a
131	cycle's SHAs at its close-out) is equally valid. The one invariant: what a rung records must be
132	permanent.
133	
134	## Preparation
135	
136	The cycle's first commit, when the cycle needs setup (a
137	lightweight cycle omits it, per
138	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)):
139	
140	- **Create the cycle's topic bookmark** (commands in
141	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
142	- **Bump the version-of-record.** Where it lives, the suffix
143	  scheme, and any derived files (a lockfile, a sourced
144	  manifest version) are project-specific. See
145	  [versioning.md](versioning.md).
146	- **Move a `## Todo` item** (if the cycle has one) into
147	  `## In Progress`, and write the cycle's **six provisional
148	  items** there. All six are required, all six are revised
149	  as steps land, and all six move to chores at close-out.
150	  The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
151	  own, and the other five are headings one level below the
152	  title (a plain cycle: `###` title, `####` items, and under
153	  a program heading, each one deeper):
154	  - the **title**, which becomes the chores section header.
155	  - the **problem statement**: what is wrong, in a sentence
156	    or two.
157	  - the **solution statement**: what will be done about it,
158	    broad. Provisional here, since it is written before the
159	    work. The close-out's commit body carries the final one.
160	  - the **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you
161	    finished?". Not the per-commit validation, which asks
162	    whether the artifact still works. This asks whether the
163	    thing the cycle promised actually happened, specifically
164	    enough that a reader can run it.
165	  - the **ladder**: one rung per step, in the form
166	    `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)` described below.
167	  - the **deliberation**: how the five above were decided,
168	    alternatives weighed, costs accepted. `_None._` when
169	    there was nothing to deliberate, which is a real answer
170	    and different from having forgotten to write it.
171	
172	The ladder is a linked table of contents. A rung is `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)` and
173	carries no detail beyond that:
174	
175	- The literal `[[N]]` is the as-built ladder's placeholder, carried from birth. It fills only
176	  at backfill after landing (see [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill)), so the close-out move
177	  just drops the `(current)` / `(done)` markers.
178	- The title links to the rung's subsection below, reference-style: `[M]` is a file-local slot
179	  whose definition is a same-file fragment, `[M]: #<slug>` in the file's `# References` (slug
180	  algorithm in [Markdown anchor links](notes.md#markdown-anchor-links)). Routing through the
181	  table keeps rung lines short, and the close-out move renumbers the slots like any other rung
182	  ref.
183	
184	The verbiage lives in the rung's subsection under a **`Ladder details`** heading following the
185	deliberation, headed by the rung's exact title, so it is greppable and an anchor other records
186	can link. Every rung has one, the close-out included, written in two beats:
187	
188	- **Opened at laddering** with an abstract-sized intent statement: the rung's problem and
189	  solution in a sentence or two, provisional like the rest of the block, so a rung nobody has
190	  started is described by more than its title.
191	- **Completed at the rung's landing** with the conceptual delta (design points, consequences,
192	  deferrals). It never restates the landed commit body's problem/solution: the body is the
193	  record, and the subsection keeps only what the body does not say.
194	
195	The closing rung differs only in its content. Its title is the cycle title plus
196	" closing" (the bookend form: [Cycle bookend titles](prose.md#cycle-bookend-titles)), it is
197	linked like its siblings, and its subsection opens at laddering with the one-line stub
198	"Closing out the cycle.", since its problem and solution are the block's own Problem and
199	Solution items. At close-out the subsection completes with what closing taught (acceptance
200	surprises, validation trip-ups, close-out-move wrinkles), written in problem/solution form, or
201	`_None._` when closing taught nothing.
202	
203	Nothing is opened in the chores file at Preparation. The
204	section is created at close-out by moving this block. See
205	[Chores sections](#chores-sections).
206	
207	**Why an acceptance check, and why it is provisional.** A
208	cycle's own per-commit checklists can all pass while its
209	banner claim is false: a seven-cycle program opened against
210	"end subprocess spawning" and its close-out claimed the goal
211	met, with about twenty spawn sites surviving, two inside the
212	facade the program built. Being provisional, the check can
213	also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
214	same failure by a slower route. So a changed check is one of
215	the things the deliberation exists to justify.
216	
217	## Work-N
218	
219	The cycle's work commits (`X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...)
220	implement the change. As many as needed:
221	
222	- Each commit runs through the
223	  **[per-commit flow](#per-commit-flow)**.
224	- **Interim pushes** are optional (backup, progress
225	  visibility).
226	- Close-out is the only mandatory push (see
227	  [Pushing](#pushing)).
228	- **Subdivide into a sub-cycle** if a Work commit's
229	  scope grows enough (see
230	  [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders)).
231	
232	## Close-out
233	
234	The cycle's last commit does bookkeeping only, and the
235	commit body describes that bookkeeping, not what happens
236	post-squash:
237	
238	- **Run the acceptance check** the Preparation stated, and
239	  record what it showed in the block, whether or not it
240	  passed. A check that was never run is a failed close-out,
241	  and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to
242	  quietly restate the banner.
243	- **Finalize the six items in place**, before the move: sync
244	  the title if the cycle's scope shifted (and every anchor
245	  back-reference), replace the provisional solution
246	  statement with what was actually done, drop the ladder's
247	  `(current)` / `(done)` markers since as-built implies
248	  done, and add any design subsections the deliberation
249	  grew. The `Ladder details` subsections ride the move
250	  unchanged.
251	- **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`,
252	  applying the four transforms in
253	  [Chores sections](#chores-sections). This *creates* the
254	  section. Nothing was opened earlier.
255	- **Write the `## Done` entry**: the version, then a bold
256	  title line with its chores `[N]` ref and detail as
257	  sub-bullets (see
258	  [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)).
259	- **Replace the `## In Progress` cycle block** with
260	  `_No cycle currently in progress._`. Under a multi-cycle
261	  program (the program heading above the cycle title) this
262	  retires the cycle's block only. The program heading and
263	  its ladder stay, the shipped rung flipped `(done)`, so the
264	  marker sits inside the program block until the next stage
265	  is picked up.
266	- **Land the cycle's bookmark** on the user's go (commands
267	  in [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
268	  Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent. Landing
269	  triggers the backfill that waits on permanence.
270	- **Update `notes/README.md`** if functionality changed
271	  (new flags, new subcommands, changed behavior).
272	
273	Whether to **squash** the cycle into one commit before the
274	publishing push, or push as-is, is decided at push time. See
275	[Pushing](#pushing).
276	
277	## Step naming
278	
279	A step has a title and no number. The ladder lists its rungs
280	in order, so position is already recorded by the list, and a
281	step is referred to by its title, verbatim-identical in the
282	ladder rung, the chores `##` header and the commit (see
283	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)).
284	A title has to be unambiguous within its cycle and within
285	its chores file, where it is also an anchor. It may repeat
286	across the repo's history.
287	
288	The version-of-record still bumps for every step, and its
289	suffix still encodes the phase, but that encoding belongs to
290	the manifest and appears nowhere in prose. It is the one
291	number left in the system, it names nothing, and nothing
292	dereferences it. The full scheme (disambiguation, nesting,
293	optional Preparation, the project's version-of-record
294	format, and the per-step bump) lives in
295	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme), which is the
296	single source of truth for this repo's versioning.
297	
298	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
299	
300	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent
301	branch. Pushing to the bookmark makes the work durable and
302	visible, but it does not publish it. Landing on the permanent
303	branch is publication, and that is the line the rules divide
304	at:
305	
306	- **Before landing**, the series should be self-consistent
307	  when practical. Inserting or reordering a step changes the
308	  ladder, and the rungs that already committed an older
309	  version of it are brought along, so the branch reads as
310	  one coherent ladder rather than a record of how it was
311	  assembled.
312	- **After landing**, the commits are history and are not
313	  touched. A recorded SHA is only ever written for a commit
314	  on a permanent branch (see
315	  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill)), which is what
316	  makes rewriting a draft safe.
317	
318	Mechanics, and why they cost so little here:
319	
320	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md`
321	  inside a rung and amending it is not a `jj describe`, so
322	  the never-re-describe rule stays intact. `ochid:` trailers
323	  survive, since they carry change ids rather than commit
324	  ids and a change id is stable across a rewrite.
325	- **Force-push the bookmark** afterwards, under the same
326	  approval any push needs.
327	- **Exceptions**, since "when practical" is not "always".
328	  Name the reason and move on:
329	  - the bookmark has already landed
330	  - another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes
331	    someone else's rebase
332	  - the ladder is long and only a trailing snapshot
333	    disagrees
334	
335	A squash-form [sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders) never
336	meets this, because nothing on it is pushed and the
337	close-out squash collapses it. The rule is for the
338	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time.
339	
340	## Per-commit flow
341	
342	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out) goes
343	through:
344	
345	1. **Mark this commit `(current)`** as the first edit in
346	   `TODO.md > ## In Progress` (`TODO.md` is at the repo
347	   root).
348	2. **Do the work** (see [Iterative work](#iterative-work)
349	   for the loop-and-squash technique).
350	3. **Flip this commit `(current)` -> `(done)`** in `## In
351	   Progress`, before the cargo cycle and the commit. Write
352	   the rung's `Ladder details` subsection now, when it has
353	   conceptual content (see [Preparation](#preparation)).
354	4. **Bump the version-of-record** to this commit's version
355	   (the suffix scheme is in
356	   [versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme)). The
357	   Preparation's own bump already covers a Preparation
358	   commit.
359	5. **Validate the artifact**, a medium-specific step. If the
360	   medium has a runnable artifact, run it at every commit,
361	   doc-only ones included: step 4 changed the version, and
362	   running it is how that is verified. For the Rust example
363	   the cargo cycle is:
364	   1. `cargo fmt`
365	   2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
366	   3. `cargo test`
367	   4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
368	   5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
369	6. **Work review.** Stop *before* writing any description,
370	   and tell the user "please review". The stop is its own
371	   message and carries no title or body, drafted or final: a
372	   description beside the work review collapses two stops
373	   into one, and describes work the review may still change.
374	   The user reviews the changes and we iterate until
375	   complete.
376	7. **Write the commit description**, only once the work
377	   review completes. See
378	   [Commit description](#commit-description).
379	8. **Commit Description review.** Show the title + body
380	   and stop. The user reviews the description. Iterate.
381	9. **Commit + push.** Hand the approved title/body to
382	   `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`, whose
383	   commit stages commit both repos and stamp the `ochid:`
384	   trailers. Never pre-commit the rung with `jj commit`: an
385	   empty `@` at push mints a stamped empty duplicate.
386	   Push approval is per-push, so step 8's
387	   review covers it only when the user's go explicitly
388	   includes the push.
389	
390	**Two overrides apply:**
391	
392	- **Deviation or question.** Any time the work deviates
393	  from the agreed plan, or a question arises, stop and
394	  surface it. Don't push through.
395	- **ESC-ESC.** The user can interrupt at any point to pull
396	  a review or question forward.
397	
398	## Commit description
399	
400	[Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/):
401	
402	```
403	<type>: <short description>
404	<type>(scope): <short description>   # optional scope
405	```
406	
407	**A commit names no version**, in its title or its body. The
408	version-of-record (where it lives and its bump cadence, see
409	[versioning.md](versioning.md)) is useful for confirming you
410	are running the version you are testing. It is not an
411	identifier, and a commit already records it in the manifest.
412	Writing it into the description copies it into text that
413	cannot be edited: a version is only stable once it lands on
414	the permanent branch, and even then a history rewrite may
415	renumber it, at which point every description naming it is
416	wrong forever. See
417	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
418	
419	### Title
420	
421	- Length per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths).
422	- Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `test`,
423	  `docs`, `chore`. Optional `(scope)` in parentheses after
424	  the type, per the spec.
425	- Favor terse phrasings.
426	- **Distinct per step.** Each of a cycle's commits gets its
427	  own descriptive title (no shared cycle title with a step
428	  marker). Share a greppable stem across the cycle's titles
429	  (e.g. `ring buffer`) so `git log --grep` collects them. The
430	  chores section header matches the close-out title. See
431	  [Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit).
432	- **Unambiguous where it is resolved**: the title is the
433	  only identifier a record has, so it must be distinct
434	  within its cycle and within its chores file (a `##` header
435	  is also an anchor). It may repeat across the repo's
436	  history. See
437	  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
438	
439	### Body
440	
441	A **problem statement** then a **solution statement**, in
442	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets), wrapped
443	per [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths).
444	The problem statement says what was wrong and defines
445	any word the title assumes. The solution statement says what
446	was done about it. How the two are arranged when the problem
447	has several facets is
448	[Commit-body form](prose.md#commit-body-form): an intro
449	paragraph, `*` bullets for facets, `-` bullets for solutions.
450	That and the rest of the content rules, including why the
451	body carries no file list, are in
452	[prose.md](prose.md#prose-form) and are not repeated here.
453	
454	Two repo-specific points:
455	
456	- **Work-repo body**: the problem is the artifact's or the
457	  records' problem.
458	- **Bot-repo (`.claude`) body**: the statements describe
459	  in-session activity rather than work-repo changes.
460	
461	### Trailer
462	
463	`ochid:` as the last line of the body. See
464	[Cross-repo linking (ochid trailers)](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)
465	in agent-data/jj.md for the convention.
466	
467	For breaking changes, use the hyphenated `BREAKING-CHANGE:`
468	trailer key. `BREAKING CHANGE:` (with a space) is the only
469	space-separated key the Conventional Commits spec allows. The
470	hyphenated form is also valid and avoids the space ambiguity.
471	
472	## Reviewing changes
473	
474	Work review looks at the **uncommitted working-copy diff**,
475	on the way to commit. The user opens diffs in their
476	editor (Zed, VSCode), and jj commands are for terminal:
477	
478	- `jj diff`: working-copy diff (uncommitted)
479	- `jj diff -r @-`: diff of the previous commit
480	- `jj diff --from <X> --to <Y>`: any two revisions
481	- `jj show -r <X>`: description + diff for one rev
482	
483	Don't `jj edit -r @-` to view a past commit, because that marks
484	it mutable and shifts `@`. Use `jj diff -r @-` or
485	`jj show -r @-`.
486	
487	No preflight while a review iterates: `fmt` / `clippy` / `test`
488	wait until the review settles, since `fmt` mutates files in ways
489	that interact badly with the user's mid-review edits. Validation
490	runs once, on the settled state, per the per-commit checklist.
491	
492	See [Sub-cycle ladders](#sub-cycle-ladders) for the
493	close-out squash recipe and recovery. Revset primitives
494	are in [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets).
495	
496	## Pushing
497	
498	### Policy
499	
500	Push is **discretionary** during the cycle (backup,
501	progress visibility) and **mandatory at close-out**, since
502	the cycle's result must be published.
503	
504	**Approval is per-push.** Every push (any repo, any kind:
505	cycle push, interim backup, recovery/surgery force-push)
506	happens only after the user has reviewed the changes to be
507	published and explicitly approved that specific push.
508	Approval of a plan that *includes* a push does not authorize
509	the push itself. Stop and ask again at the moment of pushing.
510	
511	**Default is interactive, and only an explicit scoped
512	delegation waives the gates.** The gates above (per-push approval, the
513	commit-description review that shows title+body and stops, and
514	the hard stop after push/squash-push) are the *interactive
515	default*.
516	They yield when the user **explicitly** delegates a complete,
517	bounded task and authorizes carrying it through ("do all of X
518	and push each step, don't check in"). The bot then proceeds
519	through that task's commits and pushes without stopping, and
520	continues past each push to the next step. Conditions:
521	
522	- **Explicit grant.** Never inferred from a task merely being
523	  well-scoped. The user's words must authorize unattended
524	  completion. "Commit and push" (or "then push") names the
525	  destination, not a waiver: it authorizes the push *after*
526	  the normal work review and description review, not skipping
527	  them. Only wording that explicitly waives the stops ("don't
528	  check in", "no need to review", "carry it through
529	  unattended") waives them.
530	- **Bounded goal.** Covers the named task only. It does not
531	  carry to the next task or a vaguer follow-on.
532	- **Destructive ops still pause.** Delegation covers the task's
533	  ordinary commits and pushes. It does *not* pre-authorize a
534	  genuinely irreversible action (force-push over published
535	  history, history rewrite, deleting a remote branch). Those can
536	  permanently destroy work and aren't a normal cycle step, so the
537	  bot flags one before acting. An ordinary delegated cycle never
538	  reaches this.
539	- **Still transparent.** Report each commit/push as it lands
540	  (title + outcome) so the user can catch up.
541	- **When in doubt, ask.** Ambiguous authorization falls back to
542	  per-push approval.
543	
544	**Delegation waives stops, never flow.** The stops (work review, description review, per-push
545	approval, the hard stop after the final push) are the synchronous half of review. The flow
546	(the records, the validation, the bookmark discipline) is what deferred review reads, so no
547	delegation waives it: a delegated cycle writes every record and validates every commit exactly
548	as an interactive one, and the user reviews after the fact what they would otherwise have
549	reviewed in real time. The tiers:
550	
551	- **Interactive** (the default): every stop, as above.
552	- **Delegated cycle**: rungs push to the topic bookmark without per-push asks, and `main` is
553	  untouched by construction, so review happens at landing: read the line, then land it.
554	- **Delegated project**: landing is delegated too, review happens after, and corrections
555	  become new cycles.
556	
557	Destructive ops pause in every tier, and landing is its own tier, delegated separately.
558	
559	### Shape at close-out push
560	
561	At close-out the cycle's *work* is done, and its *published
562	shape* is the remaining choice, made at push time. Surface
563	the options and get user approval before pushing. Once on
564	the target, changing shape is a remote rewrite (force-push,
565	needs approval), so choose deliberately.
566	
567	- **Squash to one commit**: single entry on the target.
568	  Right for straightforward changes where the Work-N is
569	  focused on one or two files.
570	- **Trapezoid** (a `git merge --no-ff` merge commit)
571	  *(current default)*: the target gains a merge commit
572	  (`X.Y.Z`) whose first parent is the trunk line and whose
573	  second parent is the cycle's ladder, so
574	  `git log --first-parent` reads one commit per cycle while
575	  every rung stays reachable. See
576	  [Trapezoid close-out recipe](#trapezoid-close-out-recipe)
577	  for the full sequence.
578	- **Keep separate**: one commit per cycle entry on
579	  `main`. Use when the decomposition itself is
580	  informative. Each chores section keeps its own header /
581	  ladder refs, no consolidation churn.
582	
583	A squash is set up before invoking `vc-x1 push`, while a
584	trapezoid is reshaped between two pushes (the recipe below). For any
585	other shape, drive `jj git push` directly.
586	
587	### Trapezoid close-out recipe
588	
589	A [trapezoid](#shape-at-close-out-push) close-out is
590	published in four steps: an ordinary close-out push, a
591	two-command reshape, and a second push that re-points the
592	bookmark at the reshaped commit.
593	
594	```
595	  main line   ...──<base>──────────────────<closeout>──
596	                      \                    /
597	  ladder             <rung-1>──...──<tip>─┘
598	```
599	
600	- `<base>`: the **parent of the ladder's first rung**, which
601	  is the trunk position when the cycle opened. It becomes the
602	  first parent.
603	- `<tip>`: the cycle's last Work commit. It becomes the
604	  second parent.
605	- `<closeout>`: the close-out commit, created by step 1.
606	
607	The steps. Only step 1 is a `vc-x1 push`, and the rest is
608	jj, because after step 1 the commits already exist and all
609	that remains is reshaping and publishing them:
610	
611	1. `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`
612	   - the ordinary close-out push. It commits both repos, stamps the
613	   `ochid:` trailers, and publishes `<closeout>` linearly.
614	2. `jj rebase -r <closeout> --onto <base> --onto <tip>`
615	   - `<closeout>` becomes the merge. Parent order is the
616	   argument order.
617	3. `jj new <closeout>`
618	   -  puts an empty `@` above the merge.
619	4. `jj git push --bookmark <bookmark> -R .`
620	   - publishes the reshaped commit. The bookmark needs no `jj bookmark set`:
621	   it follows the rewrite in step 2 automatically. The bot
622	   repo is untouched, and its session tail goes out with a
623	   separate `vc-x1 squash-push` afterwards.
624	
625	**Step 4 is not a `vc-x1 push`**, learned at a close-out
626	that tried it. Push runs its whole pipeline or
627	none of it, and the bot repo is never quiet for long: by the
628	time the reshape is done, `.claude` holds the session writes
629	from steps 1-3, so `commit-bot` wants to run and the message
630	stage demands a title for it. The result is a bot-side
631	requirement blocking a work-side publish that needs nothing
632	but a moved ref. Publishing an already-made commit is a
633	different operation from committing and publishing, and only
634	the latter is push's job.
635	
636	#### Details
637	
638	- **Verify two parents before step 4.** `jj log -r <closeout>
639	  -T 'parents.map(|p| p.change_id().short(8))'` must list
640	  both. jj preserves the second parent even though `<base>`
641	  is an ancestor of `<tip>` (observed at three consecutive
642	  close-outs), but a collapsed merge is indistinguishable from
643	  a correct one in `jj log --no-graph` and is only visible
644	  once published.
645	- **`<base>` is not always the previous close-out.** A docs
646	  or planning interlude between cycles sits on the trunk line
647	  and must stay there. Take the parent of the ladder's first
648	  rung, not the last close-out.
649	- **Step 3 is about `@`, not the bookmark.** The bookmark
650	  follows the rewrite in step 2 on its own. What step 2
651	  leaves misplaced is the working copy: `jj rebase -r`
652	  re-parents descendants onto the rebased commit's **old**
653	  parent, so the empty `@` from step 1 lands beside the merge
654	  on `<tip>`, and the working tree reverts to pre-close-out
655	  content, which looks alarming and isn't. `jj new` puts `@`
656	  back on top of the merge so the tree is right and the next
657	  commit continues from there. Skipping it doesn't break the
658	  publish, it just leaves you working from the wrong parent.
659	- **Trailers survive.** The reshape changes `<closeout>`'s
660	  SHA but not its change ID, so the `ochid:` trailers stamped
661	  in step 1 stay valid in both directions. This is why the
662	  reshape is safe after the trailers are written.
663	- **Step 4 moves the bookmark sideways.** Step 1's SHA
664	  becomes unreachable, and anyone who fetched between the two
665	  pushes holds a dangling commit. Consequently a
666	  [Commits backfill](#commits-backfill) must never read a
667	  SHA from that window. Wait until step 4 lands.
668	- **Immutability.** No flag is needed on a long-lived topic
669	  bookmark. Only when `<closeout>` is already on `trunk()`
670	  does the rebase need `--ignore-immutable`, and then the
671	  push force-updates the target.
672	- **The bot repo is left for afterwards.** Step 4 touches only
673	  the work repo, so `.claude` still holds every session write
674	  from the whole procedure. `vc-x1 squash-push` folds that
675	  tail into the bot commit, and its change id survives the
676	  squash, so the work-side `ochid:` keeps resolving.
677	
678	#### Recovery
679	
680	- **Nothing is published between steps 2 and 3**, so the local
681	  reshape is undoable with `jj undo` / `jj op restore`.
682	- **A collapsed or mis-parented merge** (step 2 verification
683	  fails): undo and redo step 2 with the corrected revisions.
684	  Do not push a shape you did not intend. After step 4 the
685	  remote boundary is crossed and recovery is forward-only.
686	- **Working copy left beside the merge** (step 3 skipped):
687	  `jj new <closeout>` after the fact. Nothing published is
688	  affected (the bookmark was never wrong), but any commit
689	  made in the meantime branches off `<tip>` and needs a
690	  rebase onto the merge.
691	- **A wrong bookmark position**, however it arose:
692	  `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <closeout>` before pushing.
693	  If step 4 already published it, the fix is a second
694	  sideways move, not a rewrite.
695	
696	### vc-x1 push wrapper
697	
698	`vc-x1 push <bookmark>` wraps per-push mechanics. See
699	`vc-x1 push --help` for current flags. `<bookmark>` names a
700	work-repo bookmark only. The bot repo is always pinned to
701	`main` (see [.claude cadence](#claude-cadence)).
702	
703	**Current limitation**: only fully supports the
704	[Keep separate](#shape-at-close-out-push) shape. Other
705	shapes need manual jj steps. Planned improvements are
706	project state, tracked in the project's `TODO.md`.
707	This protocol describes only the stable mechanism.
708	
709	### .claude cadence
710	
711	**Cadence**: one push = one bot-repo commit, paired
712	with every work-repo commit in that push.
713	
714	The `.claude` working copy accumulates session data
715	across the cycle. Its change ID stays stable across
716	snapshots, `jj describe`, and the squash-push fold, so
717	work-repo `ochid:` trailers resolve.
718	
719	`.claude` is a linear journal: all session work lives
720	on `main`, regardless of the work-repo bookmark. **Do
721	not create or maintain bot-repo bookmarks that mirror
722	work-repo branches**, which risks the bot steering session
723	pushes to the wrong remote ref.
724	
725	Ending a session: if the user runs `/exit` there will be
726	session information created, which we don't worry about.
727	The user can close the terminal instead and `@` will
728	remain empty.
729	
730	### Bot communication at the reviews
731	
732	Use plain prose, no insider jargon ("Gate N signal",
733	"Checkpoint N", etc.):
734	
735	- **At Work review**, summarize what changed and stop.
736	  "Work complete. Please review." No title or body in this
737	  message: the description is not yet written, and belongs
738	  to the next review.
739	- **At Commit Description review**, present `$TITLE`
740	  and `$BODY` explicitly, and ask permission to commit/push.
741	  Don't spell out the full `vc-x1 push ... --title ...
742	  --body ...` invocation by default.
743	- **At Post close-out review**, surface the shape
744	  options (squash / merge / keep) and the push target,
745	  then wait for the user's choice before any `jj squash` /
746	  `jj rebase` / `jj git push` invocation.
747	
748	### After push or squash-push: stop and wait
749	
750	After a **push** (crossing the remote boundary, by hand or
751	via the `vc-x1 push` wrapper, whose last stage publishes
752	the bot repo too) or a manual **squash-push** on the bot
753	repo, stop for the turn: no next step, edit, tool call, or
754	text output until the user directs otherwise. **Even when
755	the next step seems obvious, wait.**
756	
757	- **Scope**: the stop follows the user's directive, not the
758	  push. A standing directive covering more work ("finish
759	  the remaining ladder commits on your own") makes an
760	  intermediate push just a step, and the hard stop lands on
761	  the turn's *final* push.
762	- **Why**: the bot repo is a live journal, so everything after
763	  the invocation (its own record, closing words) lands in
764	  `@` as a trailing tail. Between delegated pushes the tail
765	  rides into the next cycle's bot commit. The final push's
766	  tail has no next commit, and the bot's own squash-push is
767	  itself session data (`@` refills immediately), so only the
768	  user, after the turn, can capture it
769	  (`vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude`).
770	- **Silence**: put all closing words *before* the final
771	  push. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a
772	  visible token after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare
773	  acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary,
774	  verification, or next-step offer. There is no "harmless"
775	  closing line after the push. That is a known slip.
776	- **Flush**: when the user wants `@` empty (no tail), they
777	  run `vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude` after the bot goes
778	  quiet, which flushes all bot session information into the
779	  published commit. Repeat if new writes land (see
780	  [Recovery](#recovery)).
781	
782	### Recovery
783	
784	- **If push exits before its last stage** (`push-work`
785	  succeeded but the bot-repo publish (`squash-push-bot`)
786	  didn't run), run the squash+push by hand:
787	
788	  ```
789	  vc-x1 squash-push -R .claude
790	  ```
791	
792	  It runs in-process, so a failure is a visible non-zero
793	  exit, with no log file to chase.
794	- **Run squash-push again if `@` is non-empty** after a
795	  pass (also desirable after extra activity by the bot's
796	  agents).
797	  - Why: the bot keeps writing session data while the
798	    command runs, so the invocation's own record plus any
799	    closing response land after the squash.
800	  - Safe to repeat: bot session data is append-only, so a
801	    re-run never conflicts or overwrites. (This could
802	    change. It is not under the user's control.)
803	  - No guarantees: events outside the bot's control can leave
804	    `@` non-empty. The bot's back end may decide to
805	    squash/consolidate session data, which can take minutes
806	    and land after the pass. The remedy is the same: just
807	    run squash-push again. This is why a single pass is never
808	    guaranteed to leave `@` empty.
809	- **Nothing to clear after an out-of-band recovery.** Push
810	  keeps no saved state, so whatever you do to the repos by
811	  hand is simply the state the next run sees.
812	- **Late work-repo tweak after the work-repo push succeeded**
813	  (e.g. updating AGENTS.md or memory) requires `jj
814	  squash --ignore-immutable` and a re-push. That is a
815	  remote rewrite and needs explicit approval like any
816	  push.
817	
818	## Iterative work
819	
820	When work for a single commit (the **target**) benefits
821	from incremental review, loop:
822	
823	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@` on top of the target.
824	2. Make the next round of changes.
825	3. User reviews the round (see
826	   [Reviewing changes](#reviewing-changes)).
827	4. `jj squash -R .` folds into the target and creates a
828	   new empty `@`.
829	5. If not done, go to step 2.
830	
831	Same jj mechanics as a
832	[sub-cycle ladder](#sub-cycle-ladders), but at
833	single-commit scope, so the version doesn't change.
834	
835	## Sub-cycle ladders
836	
837	When a Work commit subdivides into a sub-cycle (see
838	[Step naming](#step-naming), and
839	[versioning.md](versioning.md#suffix-scheme) for how the
840	manifest's suffix nests), its Work
841	commits will live as a local jj `@` chain and
842	**collapse into the sub-cycle's Close-out** before the
843	parent cycle continues. Ladder commits are scratch, for
844	review and bisection only.
845	
846	### Per-Work-commit contract within a ladder
847	
848	For each Work commit in the ladder:
849	
850	1. `jj new -R .`: create a fresh empty `@`.
851	2. Do the commit's work.
852	3. Run the fast validation (Rust example: `cargo test
853	   --bins`). **Non-negotiable**, because for code, build and
854	   clippy alone miss regressions until a later commit runs the
855	   full suite, raising bisection cost.
856	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: working title
857	   only. The sub-cycle Close-out collects everything
858	   into one final commit.
859	
860	**Nothing here is pushed.** The ladder is local until the
861	[Close-out squash](#close-out-squash-the-ladder), so no ladder
862	commit ever carries an `ochid:` trailer: the trailer is stamped
863	once, by `vc-x1 push`, on the squashed commit. Step 4 is
864	therefore first-time authoring of a scratch description, not a
865	rewrite of a published or stamped one, and is the named
866	exception to
867	[Re-describing](jj.md#re-describing-coordinate-first-and-keep-the-trailer).
868	
869	### Navigating the ladder
870	
871	Common moves:
872	
873	- `jj log -r '<base>::' -R .`: see the whole ladder
874	  from its base.
875	- `jj edit -r <prefix> -R .`: jump `@` to any ladder
876	  commit by chid prefix, useful for bisection.
877	- `jj edit @-- -R .`: quick-jump back two commits.
878	- `jj diff -r <chid> -R .`: review one commit in
879	  isolation.
880	
881	Modifications to any ladder commit rewrite it in place, and
882	descendants auto-rebase.
883	
884	### Close-out: squash the ladder
885	
886	When all ladder Work commits are done and tests pass:
887	
888	```
889	jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .
890	```
891	
892	`<base>` is the parent of the first ladder commit, and `-u`
893	keeps `@`'s description and discards the sources'.
894	After squash, history is linear (`<base> -> @`), and
895	intermediate commits are auto-abandoned.
896	
897	Then `vc-x1 push <bookmark>` as for any other commit. This is
898	the ladder's first and only publish, and where its `ochid:`
899	trailer is stamped. The scratch descriptions written at step 4
900	of the
901	[per-Work-commit contract](#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder)
902	never left the machine and never carried one, which is why
903	describing them freely is safe.
904	
905	For N = 1 the squash is a no-op (`<base>..@-` is empty
906	when `@-` is `<base>`). Push the single commit directly.
907	
908	### Recovery
909	
910	If a ladder commit goes wrong, back out without losing
911	prior commits:
912	
913	- **Discard the current commit.** `jj abandon @ -R .`
914	  drops it, and you get a fresh empty `@` on the same
915	  parent.
916	- **Edit an earlier commit.** `jj edit -r <chid> -R .`,
917	  make corrections, then `jj edit -r <last-ladder-chid>`
918	  to return. Descendants auto-rebase.
919	- **Discard the entire ladder.** `jj op log -R .` shows
920	  the op history, and `jj op restore <op-id> -R .` reverts
921	  to that point. Full undo: removes *all* ladder work
922	  after the chosen op. Use only to start over.
923	
924	# References
925	
926	- [`jj.md > Revsets`](jj.md#revsets): revset primitives
927	  (chid/cid, `@`/`@-`/`@+`, `..`/`::` ranges, prefix matching).
928	- The per-commit `cargo test --bins` gate exists because a
929	  regression introduced in an early ladder commit can go
930	  uncaught until a later commit runs the full suite, raising
931	  bisection cost.
932
